title: The real estate tax map: four moments, three kinds of tax
summary: A property deal meets tax at four moments: when land changes hands, while you build, while you operate and when you exit. Drawing that map before you price anything is the single best defence against a tax you did not see coming.
body:
Mr Shabazz, income tax is only one of the taxes on a property deal, and often not the first one you pay. Draw the map of every tax at every stage, acquisition, construction, operation and exit, before you price the land, or the map will be drawn for you by the first invoice you did not expect.

Recall

Q. Why can a partner owe tax on a partnership's profit without receiving any cash?

A. Because a flow-through entity allocates taxable profit to its partners whether or not it distributes cash. When cash goes to non-deductible loan principal, the partners face phantom income.

Q. What are the elements of negligence?

A. A duty of care owed, a breach of that duty by falling below the expected standard, harm that was caused by the breach, and harm of a kind that was reasonably foreseeable.

Q. What is the difference between levered and unlevered IRR?

A. Unlevered IRR measures the project's return on total cost as if no debt were used. Levered IRR measures the return on the equity after debt service, which leverage can raise or lower.

Why this matters

Last week was about income tax: who taxes, what kind of profit, through whom. But a developer pays tax long before there is any profit. A transfer tax at closing can be a large cheque on day one. Indirect tax on construction can be a cost or a pass-through depending on what you build. And at exit, depreciation you claimed for years can come back as taxable income. These are cash costs, they hit at specific dates, and lenders want them in the sources and uses. Elias joins me where the map crosses into income tax.

Moment one: acquisition

When land or a building changes hands, many places charge a transfer tax, a tax on the transfer of ownership of real property, usually a percentage of the price or value. It goes by many names: land transfer tax, stamp duty, registration fee. The statute usually says who is liable, often the buyer, though a contract can shift the economic burden between the parties. Some places also charge an indirect tax on the sale of land or new buildings, depending on whether the seller is in business and whether the property is new.

Applied example, hypothetical. You buy a site for 2,000,000. If a transfer tax of a hypothetical 3 percent applies, that is 60,000 due at closing, usually paid before registration can complete. It becomes part of your land cost. If you assumed it away, your equity requirement just rose by 60,000 on the day you have the least flexibility.

Moment two: construction

Most countries now have a value-added tax (VAT), called goods and services tax (GST) in some places: a tax charged at each stage of supply, where registered businesses usually recover the tax they paid on inputs through an input tax credit, a refund or offset of indirect tax paid on business purchases. The final consumer bears the tax that is not recovered.

The key question for a developer is whether what you will ultimately supply is taxable or exempt. If you build commercial space to lease, the rent is often a taxable supply, so the tax on your construction costs may be recoverable. If you build residential units to rent long-term, many systems treat the rent as exempt, which usually means the tax on your construction costs is not recoverable and becomes a real cost. The detail differs by country; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Worked example, hypothetical. Hard costs of 10,000,000 with an indirect tax of a hypothetical 10 percent, so 1,000,000 of tax on invoices. Building offices to lease, you may recover most of the 1,000,000, and it is mainly a cash-flow and timing cost. Building long-term rental apartments, you may recover little or none, and the 1,000,000 is a cost of the project. Same building shell, a 1,000,000 difference in total cost, driven by the use.

Say that out loud now.

Moment three: operation

While you own the building, three taxes usually run. Property tax, an annual levy by a local or national authority based on assessed value. Income tax on the net rent, after allowable deductions such as interest and depreciation. And indirect tax on taxable rents, which you collect from tenants and remit, or, for exempt rents, none. Property tax is an operating expense in the pro forma; income tax is below the line; indirect tax on taxable rent is usually a pass-through that must still be administered correctly.

Moment four: exit

When you sell, the income tax side has two parts. First, the gain, which may be capital or income, as you learned last week. Second, recapture: in many systems, depreciation you deducted while you owned the building is taxed back as income to the extent the sale price shows the building did not really lose that value. The indirect tax side asks whether the sale itself is taxable, which often depends on whether the building is new, residential or commercial, and whether buyer and seller are registered. The transfer tax usually falls on the buyer, but it reduces what the buyer will pay you, so it is your cost in the price.

How to draw the map

Draw a table with four columns, acquisition, construction, operation and exit, and three rows, transfer tax, indirect tax and income tax. In each cell write who pays, on what amount, when, and whether it is recoverable. Leave nothing blank: write "none" where you have confirmed none. Then give the table to a qualified adviser in the relevant country and ask them to correct it. The map is not advice; it is a list of questions in an order that makes them hard to miss.

A filled-in map, hypothetical

Here is what a first draft might look like for a hypothetical mixed-use building, shops on the ground floor and long-term rental apartments above. Every entry is an assumption to be confirmed, not a conclusion.

TaxAcquisitionConstructionOperationExit
TransferBuyer pays at closing, on priceNone confirmedNone confirmedBuyer pays; lowers our price
IndirectCheck if land sale is taxableShops: recoverable. Apartments: costShops: charge and remit. Apartments: exemptCheck per portion
IncomeNoneCapitalise costsTax on net rentGain plus recapture

Notice two things. First, the mixed use splits almost every indirect tax cell in two, which means the costs must be apportioned between the commercial and residential parts on a defensible basis, usually floor area or cost, agreed with your adviser. Second, the words "check" and "confirmed" do real work: they show the reader which cells are settled and which are still questions. A map with no open questions on it is usually a map nobody has checked.

The biggest risk

Treating indirect tax as a pass-through when, for your use, it is a cost. A residential rental developer who models construction net of indirect tax can understate total cost by the whole tax on hard costs. The control is a line in the sources and uses for unrecoverable indirect tax, set from written advice about the intended use, and a review of that line whenever the use changes. Professional sign-off required: an indirect tax specialist in the relevant country.

The beginner's mistake

Asking only "what tax will I pay on the profit?" The largest tax cheque on a project can come at closing, years before there is any profit.

Callback

In week 13 you built sources and uses, with land, hard, soft and finance costs. Every cell of today's map lands somewhere in that table: transfer tax in land, unrecoverable indirect tax in hard and soft costs, and the timing of recoverable tax in finance costs. And last week's three questions still apply at exit: recapture is income, the gain may be capital, and who pays depends on the vehicle.

Recap

Four moments: acquisition, construction, operation, exit. Three taxes: transfer, indirect, income. Transfer tax hits at closing. Indirect tax on construction is recoverable or a cost depending on what you supply. Property tax runs every year. At exit, gain and recapture. Draw the map, leave no blank cells, and get it corrected by an adviser.

Next: Ford, Failure Forensics, on a project whose margin was eaten by taxes nobody priced.
checklist: Draw a four-by-three tax map: four moments, three kinds of tax
Fill every cell with who pays, on what, when, and whether it is recoverable
Put transfer tax in the land line of sources and uses
Confirm in writing whether your end use is taxable or exempt for indirect tax
Add a line for unrecoverable indirect tax on hard and soft costs
Note the depreciation you will claim, and the recapture it may create at exit
Have an indirect tax specialist correct the map before you price the land
head: Field checklist
speak: A property deal meets tax at four moments. At acquisition, a transfer tax may be due at closing, often a percentage of the price, sometimes before registration can complete. During construction, value-added tax is charged on your inputs. Whether you get it back depends on what you will supply: commercial rents are often taxable, so tax on construction may be recoverable, while long-term residential rents are often exempt, so the tax becomes a real cost. On ten million of hard costs at a hypothetical ten percent, that is a million dollar difference. While you operate, property tax, income tax on net rent, and indirect tax on taxable rents all run. At exit, the gain may be capital or income, and depreciation you claimed may be taxed back as recapture. Draw the map, four columns and three rows, leave nothing blank, and have an adviser correct it.
terms: Transfer tax — a tax on the transfer of ownership of real property, usually a percentage of price or value
Input tax credit — a refund or offset of indirect tax a registered business paid on its business purchases
Recapture — taxing back, as income, depreciation previously deducted, to the extent the sale shows the value was not lost

hostile.q: Your hard costs are shown net of value-added tax. Are you sure you can recover it on residential rentals?
hostile.a: That is exactly the line I had checked. For the residential portion, the advice is that the tax on inputs is largely not recoverable, so it is in the budget as a cost, here, as a separate line. Only the commercial portion is modelled as recoverable, and the timing of that refund is in the finance costs. The written advice is in the appendix.

role: Failure forensics, with Cole (Audit and integrity)
title: The margin the tax map would have saved
summary: A composite case: a developer pre-sold new homes at tax-inclusive prices, assigned the land through two transfers and modelled construction net of indirect tax. Each choice looked small; together they consumed most of the profit. Taken through seven steps.
body:
Mr Shabazz, this is a composite example, built from patterns common across many projects rather than one real company. No single tax killed this project; three unpriced taxes did, each of which a one-page tax map would have shown before the first contract was signed.

Recall

Q. How do you gross up a payment to hit an after-tax target?

A. Divide the target by one minus the tax rate. Adding the rate on top gives too little.

Q. In failure forensics, why separate key decisions from assumptions?

A. Decisions are choices people made; assumptions are beliefs those choices rested on. Separating them shows whether the choice was bad or the belief was wrong, which points to a different prevention.

Q. What does an equity multiple ignore that IRR does not?

A. Time. A 1.5 times multiple earned in two years and in ten years look identical, while IRR shows the difference.

Why this matters

Failures that make headlines are usually structural or financial. Tax failures are quieter: the building gets built, the units get sold, and the developer discovers at the end that the profit went to taxes nobody put in the pro forma. Cole is with me today because every one of these was visible in the documents before signing.

The case

This is a composite example. A small developer, call him the Developer, buys a serviced site to build 40 new townhomes for sale. The land is first bought by a company he controls, then, for financing reasons, transferred to a new project company. He pre-sells the homes at prices advertised as "all-in." His pro forma shows construction costs net of indirect tax, and a margin of about 15 percent on cost, which is a thin but common target in practice, not a standard.

Step 1: Timeline

Month 0: land bought by the first company; transfer tax paid. Month 3: the lender requires a single-purpose project company, so the land is transferred again; a second transfer tax is assessed. Months 4 to 9: pre-sales close at all-in prices. Months 10 to 26: construction. Month 27: closings. Month 28: the indirect tax on the sales and the shortfall on recoverable input tax are reconciled, and the margin is found to be a fraction of the plan.

Step 2: Key decisions

Buying the land in one company and moving it to another. Advertising prices that included all taxes without computing what the tax inside the price would be. Modelling construction net of indirect tax.

Step 3: Assumptions

That a transfer between his own companies would not attract transfer tax. In some places relief exists for certain transfers between related companies, under conditions; in others it does not; he never checked. That "all-in" meant the same thing to him as to the tax authority: in a system that charges indirect tax on new homes, a tax-inclusive price contains the tax, so the developer's revenue is the price less the tax. That all input tax would be recoverable, when part of it related to things the rules treated differently.

Say that out loud now.

Step 4: Incentives

The sales agent was paid on volume and liked a simple all-in price. The lender wanted the clean project company quickly and did not care what the transfer cost. The Developer's accountant was engaged for year-end statements, not for transaction advice, and was not asked. Nobody was paid to own the tax map.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

The second land transfer produced a closing statement with a tax line on it. The sales contract template said "price includes all applicable taxes," which is a legal statement with a tax consequence. The first input tax refund claim was smaller than the model predicted. Each was a signal; each was explained away as a timing issue.

Step 6: Point of no return

The signed pre-sale contracts. Once 40 buyers held contracts at fixed tax-inclusive prices, the tax inside the price was fixed, and no later negotiation could recover it. The transfer tax was sunk at month 3. The point of no return for the whole project was the first pre-sale signature.

Step 7: Root cause

Tax was treated as an accounting task after the deal instead of a pricing input before it. The root cause is not ignorance of a rate; it is the absence of a step in the process where someone with authority asks, for each transaction, "what tax does this trigger, and who bears it?"

Cole's audit questions

Cole would have caught this with four questions at the go or no-go gate. Does any transaction move land between entities, and has transfer tax been confirmed for each move? Are sale prices stated inclusive or exclusive of indirect tax, and does the revenue line in the model match that wording? Has the recoverability of each category of input tax been confirmed in writing for the intended use? Who in the team owns the tax map, by name? Hypothetically, on 40 homes at 500,000 each, an indirect tax buried inside an all-in price at a hypothetical 10 percent tax-exclusive rate means revenue of about 454,545 per home, not 500,000: about 1,818,182 less across the project. On a 15 percent margin, that alone takes a large share of the profit.

Show your working on that: 500,000 divided by 1.10 is about 454,545, and the tax inside each price is about 45,455. Times 40 homes is about 1,818,182.

What the Developer could have done

None of the three losses required clever planning to avoid. Before buying, he could have asked his lawyer whether the land should be bought directly in a project company acceptable to the lender, removing the second transfer entirely. Before launching sales, he could have priced the homes exclusive of indirect tax, or computed the tax inside an all-in price and set the price accordingly, and used the same figure in the model. Before committing to the budget, he could have obtained written advice on which input tax was recoverable for homes built for sale and for the parts of the project treated differently. Each step was a phone call and a short memo, at a cost far below the loss.

The deeper fix is organisational. On a small team, one named person owns the tax map, keeps it current at each gate, and must sign it before any price list, land agreement or intercompany transfer goes out. That is not bureaucracy; it is the same discipline as a hold point on a construction site, applied to money.

The biggest risk

A contract that fixes the tax treatment before anyone has analysed it. Sales contracts, land agreements and intercompany transfers all have tax consequences in their wording. The control is that no price is quoted and no transfer is signed until the tax map for that transaction is written and reviewed. Professional sign-off required: an indirect tax specialist and a real estate lawyer in the relevant country.

The beginner's mistake

Thinking that moving land between your own companies is an internal bookkeeping step. To a tax authority, it is usually a transfer like any other unless a specific relief applies and its conditions are met.

Rule 23

Rule 23: No price is quoted and no transfer is signed until the tax map for that transaction is written down: who pays what, on which amount, and when.

Callback

In week 20 you learned that contract wording decides what binds. "Price includes all applicable taxes" binds the developer to absorb the tax. And in week 13, contingency was for unknowns; a tax you could have computed is not an unknown, and it should never be paid out of contingency.

Recap

Two transfers, two transfer taxes. All-in prices that hid the indirect tax inside revenue. Construction modelled net of tax that was only partly recoverable. The point of no return was the first signed pre-sale. Root cause: tax as an afterthought. Rule 23 puts the map before the price.

Next: Nadia, The Money, on how transaction taxes move cost, yield and value.
checklist: List every transaction that moves land, and confirm transfer tax for each
Check whether any relief for related-company transfers applies, and its conditions
State in every sales contract whether prices include or exclude indirect tax
Make the revenue line in the model match the contract wording
Confirm in writing which input tax is recoverable for the intended use
Name the person who owns the tax map
Do not pay a computable tax out of contingency
head: Field checklist
speak: This is a composite case. A developer buys land in one company, then moves it to a new project company because the lender wants one, and pays transfer tax twice, because nobody checked whether the internal move was relieved. He pre-sells forty new homes at prices described as all-in, which means the indirect tax is inside his revenue. At a hypothetical ten percent, a 500,000 price carries about 45,455 of tax, so across forty homes his revenue is about 1.8 million lower than planned. And he models construction net of indirect tax that turns out to be only partly recoverable. The point of no return was the first signed pre-sale, because the tax inside a fixed price cannot be recovered later. The root cause was treating tax as an accounting task after the deal. Rule 23: no price quoted and no transfer signed until the tax map is written down.
terms: Tax-inclusive price — a price that already contains the indirect tax, so the seller's revenue is the price less the tax
Related-company transfer relief — a relief, where it exists, that reduces or removes transfer tax on moves between connected companies under conditions
Tax map — a written table of every tax a transaction triggers: who pays, on what amount, when, and whether it is recoverable

hostile.q: Your sales contracts say all applicable taxes are included. How much of the price is actually yours?
hostile.a: The model computes revenue as the price divided by one plus the indirect tax rate, so the tax inside the price is already removed. On a 500,000 home at the working rate, that is about 454,545 of revenue. The rate is provisional and the contract wording has been reviewed by our lawyer and an indirect tax specialist.

rule: Rule 23: No price is quoted and no transfer is signed until the tax map for that transaction is written down: who pays what, on which amount, and when.

title: How transaction taxes move cost, yield and value
summary: Transfer tax, unrecoverable indirect tax and recapture each change a different number: total cost, yield on cost, and the cash you keep at exit. This lesson works each one through the pro forma with hypothetical figures.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a transaction tax is never just a cost line; it moves your yield on cost, your equity requirement, your financing and your exit cheque, each in a different way. Model each one where it actually lands, and the deal you see will be the deal you get.

Recall

Q. What is Rule 23?

A. No price is quoted and no transfer is signed until the tax map for that transaction is written down: who pays what, on which amount, and when.

Q. Why does liability insurance appear in a pro forma as more than a premium?

A. Because deductibles, exclusions and uninsured exposure are real costs too. The premium is only the visible part of the cost of risk.

Q. What is cash-on-cash return?

A. Annual pre-tax cash flow to equity divided by the equity invested, a simple yearly measure that ignores time value and the exit.

Why this matters

Your go or no-go decision often turns on yield on cost, stabilised net operating income (NOI) divided by total project cost, compared with the market cap rate. The gap between them is the development spread you met in week 10. Transaction taxes sit inside total cost, so they change the spread directly. A tax you leave out can make a deal look as if it clears the spread when it does not.

Transfer tax and indirect tax change total cost

Worked example one, hypothetical round numbers. A 60-unit rental building.

  1. Land: 2,000,000. Transfer tax at a hypothetical 3 percent: 60,000.
  2. Hard costs before indirect tax: 9,000,000. Indirect tax at a hypothetical 10 percent: 900,000.
  3. Soft and finance costs: 2,000,000, with indirect tax on the soft-cost portion of a hypothetical 100,000.

Version A, the indirect tax is wrongly treated as fully recoverable: total cost is 2,000,000 plus 60,000 plus 9,000,000 plus 2,000,000, which is 13,060,000. Version B, the residential rents are exempt so the indirect tax is not recoverable: total cost adds 900,000 and 100,000, giving 14,060,000.

Stabilised NOI is 900,000. Yield on cost in Version A is 900,000 divided by 13,060,000, about 6.89 percent. In Version B it is 900,000 divided by 14,060,000, about 6.40 percent. If the market cap rate for this kind of building is a hypothetical 5.75 percent, the spread falls from about 114 basis points to about 65. A basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point. Many developers would treat a spread near 150 basis points as a common target in practice, not a standard; Version B may fail your own gate while Version A passes it.

Say that out loud now.

Timing changes financing

Even where indirect tax is recoverable, it is paid to suppliers first and recovered later, often weeks or months after each filing period. That gap must be financed. If the lender will not fund recoverable tax, your equity carries it. Worked example two, hypothetical: on a commercial project, recoverable input tax of 800,000 is paid evenly over 16 months, 50,000 a month, and each month's tax is refunded about 3 months later. At the peak, about 150,000 is outstanding. If it is funded at a hypothetical 8 percent a year, the carrying cost over the period is modest, but the 150,000 peak must be in the equity or a facility from day one. Leaving it out creates a cash squeeze in month four, exactly when contractors expect to be paid.

Recapture changes the exit cheque

Suppose, hypothetically, you claimed 1,200,000 of depreciation on the building over the hold. Each year, that deduction reduced your taxable income. At sale, if the building is sold for more than its depreciated tax value, many systems tax back the depreciation as income. If recapture is taxed at a hypothetical 40 percent, that is 480,000 due at exit. If you modelled exit tax only on the capital gain, you have understated the tax by up to 480,000. The deduction was not free money; much of it was a loan from the tax authority, repayable at sale.

Value is cut too, not only cost

Transaction taxes also act on value through the buyer. A buyer who must pay transfer tax on top of the price treats it as part of their cost of acquisition, so the price they can offer for a target return falls by roughly the tax. Worked example three, hypothetical: a buyer will pay whatever gives a 5.75 percent yield on their total cost. NOI of 900,000 divided by 0.0575 gives a total cost of about 15,652,000. If the buyer faces transfer tax of a hypothetical 3 percent on the price, then price times 1.03 must equal 15,652,000, so the price is about 15,196,000. The tax, about 456,000, comes out of what you receive, even though the buyer writes the cheque.

This is why experienced sellers think about the buyer's tax costs as well as their own. It is not generosity; it is understanding what the buyer can afford to pay. If a structure exists that lawfully reduces the buyer's transfer tax, such as a sale of shares in the owning company rather than the land, in places where that is treated differently, the saving may be shared through price. Whether that is available, and its consequences for both sides, is a question for advisers in the relevant country.

How the best do it

Disciplined institutional developers keep a separate indirect tax cash flow alongside the construction cash flow, showing tax paid, tax recovered and the timing gap, month by month, and size the equity or facility to the peak. They also run a tax-adjusted sources and uses that shows unrecoverable indirect tax as its own line, so a reviewer can see in one glance whether the team has assumed recovery. A small developer can copy both with two extra rows in the model.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note: every property on your personal balance sheet carries two hidden liabilities. The deferred tax on any unrealised gain, which you met last week, and the recapture built into depreciation already claimed. A building you have depreciated heavily may look like a great after-tax performer year by year, while quietly growing a tax bill payable at sale. List both, so that your net worth is honest and your decisions about refinancing, selling or gifting are made on the right number.

Order of operations in the model

Put the lines in the order the money moves. Land, then transfer tax. Hard costs net of tax, then recoverable tax with its timing, then unrecoverable tax as a cost. Soft and finance costs, including the cost of carrying the recoverable tax. Then total cost, then yield on cost, then the spread. At exit: price, the buyer's transfer tax reflected in that price, selling costs, recapture, capital gain, tax, debt repayment and net cash. A reviewer should be able to read down the sheet and see every tax at the moment it is paid. If a tax appears only inside a blended percentage somewhere, move it into its own line.

The biggest risk

Mixing up recoverable and unrecoverable indirect tax in the same line, so that nobody can see which assumption the model makes. The control is separate lines for recoverable tax, with its timing, and unrecoverable tax, as a cost, each tied to written advice about the end use. Professional sign-off required: an indirect tax specialist and the project accountant.

The beginner's mistake

Treating depreciation as a permanent saving. Often it is a deferral that partly reverses at sale.

Callback

In week 10 you learned the development spread: yield on cost minus market cap rate. Today you saw a 1,000,000 tax line cut that spread by about 49 basis points. And in week 15, after-tax leakage: recapture is one of its biggest sources, and it arrives in the very year you were planning to celebrate.

Recap

Transfer tax and unrecoverable indirect tax raise total cost and cut yield on cost. Recoverable indirect tax still costs money to carry. Depreciation claimed now can be recaptured at sale. Model each where it lands, keep recoverable and unrecoverable separate, and carry recapture on your personal balance sheet.

Next: Devika, The Rules, on who is legally liable for each tax, and how Canada and Guyana approach it.
checklist: Put transfer tax in land cost, not contingency
Split indirect tax into recoverable and unrecoverable lines
Recompute yield on cost with unrecoverable tax included
Model the timing gap on recoverable tax and size equity to the peak
Ask the lender whether it funds recoverable indirect tax
Model recapture at exit separately from the capital gain
Carry deferred tax and recapture on your personal balance sheet
head: Field checklist
speak: Transaction taxes move different numbers. Transfer tax and unrecoverable indirect tax raise total cost, which cuts yield on cost. In a hypothetical 60-unit rental, treating indirect tax as recoverable gave a total cost of 13.06 million and a yield on cost near 6.89 percent. With the tax correctly treated as a cost, total cost was 14.06 million and yield fell to about 6.40 percent. Against a hypothetical 5.75 percent cap rate, the spread shrank from about 114 to 65 basis points, enough to fail a go gate. Even recoverable tax costs money, because you pay it before you get it back, and the peak must be funded. At exit, depreciation you claimed may be taxed back as recapture, so model it separately from the gain. And on your personal balance sheet, carry both the deferred tax and the recapture, so your net worth is honest.
terms: Yield on cost — stabilised net operating income divided by total project cost
Basis point — one hundredth of one percentage point
Timing gap — the period between paying recoverable indirect tax and receiving it back, which must be financed

hostile.q: Your yield on cost assumes construction costs net of value-added tax. Show me where the unrecoverable tax is.
hostile.a: It is the separate line under hard costs, 900,000, plus 100,000 under soft costs, based on written advice that the residential rents are exempt. With it, yield on cost is about 6.40 percent, and that is the figure in the go decision. The recoverable portion on the commercial ground floor is modelled separately with its timing gap in the finance costs.

title: Who is liable, and what the contract can change
summary: The statute decides who owes a tax to the authority; the contract can only decide who bears it between the parties. This lesson covers liability, taxable and exempt supplies, change of use and recapture in concept, then compares how Canada and Guyana approach the point.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a contract can move the cost of a tax between buyer and seller, but it usually cannot move the legal liability to pay it to the authority. Know which person the statute names, then use the contract to decide who ends up paying.

Recall

Q. What facts point a gain toward capital rather than business income?

A. An intention to hold recorded at purchase, long-term financing, a long holding period, no history of similar quick sales, and no subdivision or marketing activity. The facts decide, not the label.

Q. When might a court pierce the corporate veil?

A. When a company is used as a sham, a mere façade or an instrument to commit a wrong or evade an existing obligation. Ordinary use of limited liability is not enough.

Q. What is after-tax leakage?

A. The difference between the return a project earns and the return its owners keep after every layer of tax.

Why this matters

Every purchase and sale agreement has a tax clause, and most developers skim it. The clause decides who bears transfer tax, whether the price includes indirect tax, who is responsible if the authority later disagrees, and how the price is split between land and building. That split alone can move hundreds of thousands of dollars between the two sides. You need to know what the law fixes and what you can negotiate.

Liability versus burden

The statute that creates a tax usually says who is liable to the authority: for a transfer tax, often the buyer or the person registering the transfer; for indirect tax on a sale, often the seller, who must charge, collect and remit it, though some systems reverse this for certain property sales so the registered buyer self-assesses. That is legal liability. The contract can then say that the other party will reimburse or indemnify, which moves the economic burden. If the reimbursing party fails to pay, the authority usually still pursues the person the statute names. So a clause shifting tax to an unreliable counterparty gives you a claim, not protection. Verify which party is liable in each case against the primary source.

Applied example, hypothetical. You sell a commercial building to a buyer who agrees the price is "exclusive of indirect tax" and promises to pay any indirect tax on top. If, under the local rules, you as seller must collect and remit, and the buyer never pays the tax portion, you may still owe it. The protection is to collect the tax at closing through the lawyers' trust account, not to rely on a promise.

Taxable, exempt and zero-rated, and why use matters

In most value-added tax systems, a supply is taxable (tax charged, input tax recoverable), exempt (no tax charged, input tax usually not recoverable) or zero-rated (tax charged at zero, input tax usually recoverable). Real estate is full of distinctions: new versus used residential, residential versus commercial, sale versus lease, short-term versus long-term occupancy. Because recoverability follows use, a change of use, for example from offices to apartments, can require past input tax credits to be repaid or adjusted. Some systems also deem a builder who rents out new homes it built, instead of selling them, to have sold them to itself at fair market value, triggering tax; this is often called a self-supply rule. Canada has rules of this kind for new residential rental property. Verify the current rule against the primary source before you rely on it.

Say that out loud now.

Recapture and the purchase price allocation

Depreciation for tax is claimed on buildings and equipment, not on land. So when a property is sold for one price, the contract or the parties must split it between land, building and sometimes equipment: the purchase price allocation. The seller generally prefers less allocated to the depreciated building, which can reduce recapture. The buyer generally prefers more allocated to building, which gives a larger base for future depreciation. Authorities may challenge an allocation that does not reflect value. The practical rule: agree the allocation in the contract, support it with an appraisal, and make sure both parties file consistently. Tomorrow Elias works the numbers.

Two Systems: Canada and Guyana

A conceptual comparison only; verify against primary source before relying on any of it. Canada levies a federal goods and services tax, harmonised with provincial sales tax in some provinces, under which sales of new residential property are generally taxable, long-term residential rents are generally exempt, and commercial rents are generally taxable; land transfer taxes are levied at the provincial and sometimes municipal level, so the rules differ by province; and capital gains and recapture are dealt with under federal income tax legislation. Guyana operates a value-added tax administered by the Guyana Revenue Authority, and taxes certain capital gains under separate legislation from its income tax; how a land transfer is charged on registration, and how residential property, rents and sales are treated for value-added tax, must be read in the current statutes and guidance. The structural lesson is that two systems can both tax a property deal at four moments while splitting liability, exemptions and relief very differently. Professional sign-off required: a tax adviser qualified in each country.

Reading the tax clause: six checks

  1. Is the price inclusive or exclusive of indirect tax, in plain words?
  2. Who bears transfer tax, and is it collected at closing?
  3. Is the purchase price allocation stated, and is it supported by valuation?
  4. Who bears tax if the authority later reassesses the treatment?
  5. Are there representations on the seller's registration status and the property's tax history, such as past credits claimed?
  6. Is there a cooperation clause requiring both sides to file consistently and share documents?

A worked clause, hypothetical

Here is how a short, clear tax clause might read in plain words, as an illustration of the concepts rather than a drafting precedent: "The purchase price is 14,000,000 and excludes indirect tax. Indirect tax, if payable on any portion of the sale, shall be paid by the buyer at closing through the vendor's solicitor's trust account. The parties allocate the purchase price as 4,500,000 to land and 9,500,000 to building, as supported by an independent appraisal, and shall each file their returns consistently with that allocation. The buyer shall pay any transfer tax payable on registration." Each sentence answers one cell of the map. A lawyer must draft the real clause for the relevant jurisdiction; your job is to know what each sentence must achieve and to notice when one is missing.

Notice also what that sample clause does not say. It does not promise a tax result, such as "the sale is exempt," because neither party can guarantee how the authority will treat it. A clause that promises a result is a representation, and if it turns out wrong it can become a claim against whoever gave it. Keep promises to facts you control, and let the advice cover the rest.

The biggest risk

An indemnity from a party who cannot pay. The control is to collect tax at closing through an escrow or trust account wherever possible, and to treat any indemnity as security only as good as the person giving it. Professional sign-off required: a real estate lawyer and an indirect tax specialist.

The beginner's mistake

Leaving the allocation of price to the accountants after closing. Once signed without it, you have lost the moment when it could be negotiated.

Callback

In week 21 you learned the difference between being liable and being able to pass a loss on through indemnities and insurance. Tax works the same way: the statute fixes liability, the contract moves burden, and the burden only moves if the other party can pay. And last week, flow-through entities moved income tax to owners; today the contract moves transaction tax between parties.

Recap

The statute names who is liable; the contract moves the burden. Taxable, exempt and zero-rated supplies decide whether input tax is recoverable, and a change of use can claw back credits. Allocation of price between land and building pits seller against buyer on recapture and depreciation. Canada and Guyana both tax property transactions, structured differently; verify both.

Next: Elias, The Numbers, working a full exit tax calculation step by step.
checklist: Identify who the statute makes liable for each tax, separately from the contract
Collect tax at closing through escrow or trust where possible
State plainly whether the price includes or excludes indirect tax
Agree the land and building allocation in the contract, with a valuation
Check whether a change of use could claw back past input tax credits
Ask whether a self-supply rule applies if you rent instead of sell
Include a cooperation clause for consistent filing
head: Field checklist
speak: The statute decides who owes a tax to the authority. The contract can only decide who bears it between buyer and seller. If the person who promised to reimburse you does not pay, the authority usually still comes to the person the statute names, so collect tax at closing rather than relying on a promise. In value-added tax, supplies are taxable, exempt or zero-rated, and that decides whether tax on your inputs is recoverable. Because recoverability follows use, changing a building from offices to apartments can claw back past credits, and some systems tax a builder who rents out new homes as if it sold them to itself. The price on a sale must also be split between land and building. Sellers usually want less on the building to limit recapture; buyers want more for future depreciation. Agree it in the contract, support it with a valuation, and verify every rule.
terms: Legal liability — the obligation, set by statute, to pay a tax to the authority
Economic burden — who ends up bearing the cost of a tax after the contract allocates it
Purchase price allocation — the split of a sale price between land, building and equipment, which drives recapture and future depreciation

hostile.q: The buyer has agreed to indemnify you for any transfer and indirect tax. Why are you still insisting it be paid at closing?
hostile.a: Because the indemnity moves the cost, not the liability. If the authority comes to us and the buyer's company has been wound up, the indemnity is worth nothing. Paying through the lawyers' trust account at closing costs the buyer nothing extra and removes a risk we cannot price.

title: An exit, taxed line by line
summary: A full worked exit for a hypothetical stabilised building: purchase allocation, depreciation, sale allocation, recapture, capital gain, selling costs, tax and net cash. Then the same sale with a different allocation, to show what the negotiation is really about.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the exit cheque is the number you build the whole project to reach, and it is made of several different kinds of tax on several different kinds of gain. Work it line by line once with your own hands, and you will never accept a single blended exit tax figure again.

Recall

Q. What are the four moments on the real estate tax map?

A. Acquisition, construction, operation and exit. At each one, check transfer tax, indirect tax and income tax.

Q. What does a personal guarantee add to your exposure?

A. It makes you personally liable for the guaranteed debt up to the guaranteed amount, beyond the equity you invested.

Q. How do you compute IRR for a single investment and a single return?

A. Divide the return by the investment, raise the result to one over the number of years, and subtract one.

Why this matters

Investors, lenders and buyers will all quote you exit figures. If you cannot rebuild the after-tax cash from the sale price, you cannot tell whether a proposed allocation, a buyer's term or a hold-versus-sell recommendation is good for you. Every rate here is hypothetical and chosen for arithmetic; verify real rates and rules against the primary source before you rely on them. Many systems differ on whether recapture applies, how gains are taxed and how selling costs are treated.

The facts, hypothetical

  • Purchase price: 10,000,000, allocated 3,000,000 to land and 7,000,000 to building.
  • Depreciation claimed on the building over six years: 1,400,000 in total. Land is not depreciated.
  • So the building's undepreciated tax cost is 7,000,000 minus 1,400,000, which is 5,600,000.
  • Sale price: 14,000,000, allocated 4,500,000 to land and 9,500,000 to building.
  • Selling costs: 300,000. Loan payoff at closing: 6,000,000.
  • Hypothetical rates: recapture taxed as income at 40 percent; capital gains at an effective 20 percent.

Step by step

  1. Recapture on the building. In this hypothetical system, recapture is the lesser of the building's proceeds and its original cost, minus its undepreciated cost. The lesser of 9,500,000 and 7,000,000 is 7,000,000. Minus 5,600,000 gives recapture of 1,400,000. All the depreciation comes back, because the building sold for more than it cost.
  2. Capital gain on the building: proceeds 9,500,000 minus original cost 7,000,000 gives 2,500,000.
  3. Capital gain on the land: 4,500,000 minus 3,000,000 gives 1,500,000.
  4. Selling costs, deducted from the capital gain in this hypothetical: total capital gain 2,500,000 plus 1,500,000 minus 300,000 gives 3,700,000.
  5. Check: total economic gain is sale price 14,000,000, less selling costs 300,000, less the tax cost of what was sold, 3,000,000 plus 5,600,000, which is 8,600,000. That leaves 5,100,000. Recapture 1,400,000 plus capital gain 3,700,000 is 5,100,000. It ties out.
  6. Tax on recapture: 1,400,000 times 40 percent is 560,000.
  7. Tax on capital gain: 3,700,000 times 20 percent is 740,000.
  8. Total tax: 1,300,000.
  9. Net cash: 14,000,000 minus 300,000 selling costs, minus 6,000,000 loan payoff, minus 1,300,000 tax, gives 6,400,000.

Say that out loud now.

The same sale, a different allocation

The buyer proposes 11,000,000 to building and 3,000,000 to land, because a bigger building value gives the buyer more depreciation. What happens to you?

  1. Recapture: the lesser of 11,000,000 and 7,000,000 is 7,000,000, minus 5,600,000, still 1,400,000. Recapture is capped at original cost, so it does not change.
  2. Building gain: 11,000,000 minus 7,000,000 is 4,000,000. Land gain: 3,000,000 minus 3,000,000 is zero. Total capital gain: 4,000,000 minus 300,000 is 3,700,000, the same.
  3. Your tax is unchanged at 1,300,000. In this hypothetical you can give the buyer what he wants at no cost to you, and you should ask for something in return.

Now the opposite: you propose only 6,500,000 to building and 7,500,000 to land.

  1. Recapture: the lesser of 6,500,000 and 7,000,000 is 6,500,000, minus 5,600,000, giving 900,000.
  2. Building: proceeds 6,500,000 are below original cost 7,000,000, so no capital gain on the building. Land gain: 7,500,000 minus 3,000,000 is 4,500,000. Capital gain after selling costs: 4,200,000.
  3. Tax: 900,000 times 40 percent is 360,000, plus 4,200,000 times 20 percent is 840,000. Total 1,200,000, which is 100,000 less than before.

But the buyer now has a smaller building base to depreciate, so he will push back or lower the price. And an authority may challenge an allocation that does not match value. That is why the allocation must be supported by an independent valuation.

Where the indirect tax fits

If part of the building is commercial and that part of the sale is a taxable supply, indirect tax may be charged on top of the price for that portion and remitted by whoever the statute names. For a registered buyer who can recover it, it is mainly a cash-flow item at closing, but it must be collected at closing, or it becomes your cost. Leave a line for it in the closing statement and confirm the treatment in writing.

From net cash to multiple and IRR

Suppose, hypothetically, your equity at purchase was 4,000,000, and you ignore interim cash flow to keep it simple. Pre-tax cash to equity at exit was 14,000,000 minus 300,000 minus 6,000,000, which is 7,700,000. The pre-tax multiple is 7,700,000 divided by 4,000,000, about 1.93 times. After tax, net cash of 6,400,000 gives about 1.60 times. Over a six-year hold, the pre-tax IRR is about 11.5 percent and the after-tax IRR about 8.1 percent, because 1.93 to the power of one sixth is about 1.115, and 1.60 to the power of one sixth is about 1.081.

That gap of more than three points is what a single blended rate tends to blur. Notice also where the 1,300,000 of tax came from: 560,000 of it was recapture, tax on deductions you enjoyed in earlier years. If those earlier years were shown in the model at their after-tax cash, you saw the benefit; the exit is where the bill arrives. Showing both sides in one place is what makes the after-tax IRR honest.

Three questions to ask your adviser

  1. In this country, is recapture computed the way this hypothetical computes it, capped at original cost, or differently, and at what rate is it taxed? Verify against the primary source.
  2. Are selling costs deducted from the gain, from recapture, or apportioned between them, and are any of them recoverable for indirect tax?
  3. Does selling shares in the owning company instead of the building change the recapture, the gain or the transfer tax, for us and for the buyer?

The third question is the bridge to exit structuring, which you will study properly in week 64. Asking it early costs nothing, and the answer may change how you hold the building from day one, because some choices about the holding vehicle cannot be made at the point of sale. Write the adviser's answers into the model's assumption sheet with the date and the name of the person who gave them, so that the next reviewer knows which numbers are confirmed and which are still provisional.

The biggest risk

A single blended exit tax rate in the model, which hides recapture and makes allocation invisible. The control is the line-by-line calculation above, with a tie-out, built into the model and reviewed by an adviser before you accept an offer. Professional sign-off required: a tax adviser in the relevant country, and an appraiser for the allocation.

The beginner's mistake

Forgetting that land is not depreciated, so all depreciation sits on the building, and the building's allocation decides how much of it comes back.

Callback

In week 15 you learned that IRR and multiple are usually shown before tax. Today's 1,300,000 of exit tax on a 5,100,000 gain shows how far the after-tax multiple can sit below the pre-tax one. And yesterday, the contract decided who bears tax; here, one contract clause, the allocation, decided 100,000.

Recap

Recapture 1,400,000, capital gain 3,700,000, tax 1,300,000, net cash 6,400,000, with a tie-out. Shifting value to the building cost the seller nothing here because recapture is capped at cost. Shifting value to land saved the seller 100,000 but costs the buyer depreciation. Verify every rule and rate.

Next: Devika, The Room, negotiating the tax clause at the closing table.
checklist: Record the land and building split at purchase
Track depreciation claimed and the building's undepreciated tax cost
Compute recapture and capital gain separately at exit
Tie out recapture plus gain to the total economic gain
Test the effect of different allocations on both sides
Support any allocation with an independent valuation
Put indirect tax on the sale as its own closing-statement line
head: Field checklist
speak: Here is a hypothetical exit worked line by line. Bought for ten million, three to land, seven to building. Depreciation claimed: 1.4 million, so the building's undepreciated cost is 5.6 million. Sold for fourteen million, 4.5 to land and 9.5 to building, with 300,000 selling costs. Recapture is the lesser of proceeds and original cost, seven million, less 5.6 million: 1.4 million, all of it. Capital gain is 2.5 million on the building and 1.5 million on the land, less 300,000: 3.7 million. Together that is 5.1 million, which ties to the total gain. At hypothetical rates of 40 and 20 percent, tax is 560,000 plus 740,000: 1.3 million. After the six million loan, net cash is 6.4 million. Shift value to land and the seller saves 100,000, but the buyer loses depreciation. Always support the allocation with a valuation.
terms: Undepreciated tax cost — an asset's original tax cost less the depreciation already claimed
Tie-out — a check figure proving that two calculations agree
Allocation — the split of one price between assets taxed differently, such as land and building

hostile.q: Your exit model shows one tax line at 20 percent of the gain. Where is the recapture?
hostile.a: You are right that a single line hides it. The revised model splits the exit into recapture of 1.4 million, taxed as income, and a capital gain of 3.7 million, with a tie-out to the total gain of 5.1 million. At the provisional rates, total exit tax is 1.3 million, not 1.02 million, and the rates are being verified by our adviser.

title: The tax clause at the closing table
summary: A scene: the buyer's lawyer proposes a price inclusive of all taxes, an allocation weighted to the building and an indemnity in place of payment at closing. The lines to say, the lines never to say, and the question behind each request.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the closing table is where tax wording turns into money, and it is usually the last place anyone expects a negotiation. Arrive with your tax map, your allocation and your walk-away points already written, and you will spend the meeting listening instead of calculating.

Recall

Q. What is Rule 23?

A. No price is quoted and no transfer is signed until the tax map for that transaction is written down: who pays what, on which amount, and when.

Q. In a room where liability is being argued, why avoid admitting fault in the first meeting?

A. Because an admission can be used later and may affect insurance coverage. You can acknowledge the problem and commit to fixing it without conceding legal fault.

Q. What does a sensitivity on exit cap rate tell an investor?

A. How much the value and return change if the market prices the building at a higher or lower cap rate at sale, which is often the single largest driver of return.

Why this matters

Most of a sale agreement is settled by lawyers over weeks. The tax clause often is not. It arrives late, it looks technical, and the other side counts on you being tired and eager to close. Yet in yesterday's numbers, one allocation choice moved 100,000, and a price wording choice can move far more. This scene is how to hold the line without blowing up the deal.

The scene

This is a hypothetical scene. You are selling a mixed-use building: ground-floor shops and apartments above. The price is agreed at 14,000,000. The buyer's lawyer opens the final draft and says three things. One: "We've put the price as inclusive of all taxes, to keep it simple." Two: "We've allocated 11,000,000 to the building, which our appraiser supports." Three: "Instead of collecting the indirect tax on the commercial portion at closing, our client will indemnify you. It's a cash-flow point for them."

The lines to say

  • On the price: "We agreed 14,000,000 as the price of the property. Indirect tax, where it applies, is in addition. Let's write it exclusive and state the tax treatment of each portion."
  • On the allocation: "Our numbers show the building allocation doesn't change our tax, so we can accept it. It is valuable to your client, so let's talk about what we get for it."
  • On the indemnity: "We need the indirect tax collected through the trust account at closing. An indemnity moves the cost, but if the authority comes to us, we're the ones liable."
  • "Can you walk me through how your client's lender treats this? If the lender won't fund it, let's solve that rather than move the risk to us."
  • "Let's confirm both sides will file consistently with this allocation, and add a cooperation clause."

Say that out loud now.

The lines never to say

  • "Inclusive is fine." On a taxable portion, inclusive means the tax comes out of your 14,000,000.
  • "Whatever allocation works for you." You have just given away something of value for nothing.
  • "I trust your client." This is not about trust; the statute decides who the authority pursues.
  • Any statement of a rate or a rule as fact. Say "our adviser's position is" and point to the written advice.

The question behind the question

"To keep it simple" usually means "to keep the tax out of our cash at closing." "Our appraiser supports it" usually means "we want depreciation and expect you not to notice it costs you nothing to give." "It's a cash-flow point" usually means the buyer's financing does not cover the indirect tax at closing, which is a real problem, but it is theirs. The respectful answer to each is to name the real issue and solve it, rather than accept the framing. For the cash-flow point, a solution may be closing on a date that lets the buyer recover the tax quickly, if the rules allow, or a short bridge from the buyer's side.

When to stay silent

After you say "it's valuable to your client, so let's talk about what we get for it," stop. Do not fill the silence with a suggestion. The other lawyer will either offer something, such as a shorter closing period, a reduced holdback or a cleaner representation, or will reveal how much the allocation matters to them. Either outcome is information you can use.

Holding your state

Closings are long and tiring, and fatigue makes people agree to wording to end the meeting. Know your walk-away points before you arrive, on one card: price exclusive of indirect tax, tax collected at closing, allocation consistent with a valuation, cooperation clause. If a request touches one of those, slow down and say, "Let me check that against our numbers," then check it. A short break is a normal part of a closing; taking one shows control, not weakness.

If they push back

Suppose the buyer's lawyer replies: "If you insist on collecting the tax at closing, my client will need a reduced price to cover the financing." Do not argue the principle again; you have stated it. Move to numbers. Ask how much the financing cost actually is, for how long, and why the lender will not fund it. If the amount is modest, a small contribution may close the deal cleanly while keeping the liability where it belongs. If the request is a disguised price cut, it will show, because the number will be far larger than any plausible carrying cost.

A useful line is: "Help me understand the size of the problem. If it's a few weeks of carrying cost on the tax, let's put a number on it." That keeps the conversation commercial and respectful. If the other side cannot produce a number, the problem was never the financing. You can then return calmly to your card: price exclusive, tax collected at closing, allocation supported by valuation, cooperation clause. Many closings stall on tax wording for an hour and then settle exactly where a well-prepared seller started, because the prepared seller was the only one in the room with the numbers.

After the meeting

Within the hour, send a short email to both lawyers recording what was agreed on each tax point, in the order of your card: price exclusive of indirect tax, tax collected at closing through the trust account, allocation and the valuation supporting it, the cooperation clause, and anything traded for the allocation. Ask the other side to confirm by reply. This is not distrust; it is the habit of writing down a decision while everyone still remembers it the same way, which saves arguments when the final draft arrives at midnight before closing.

The biggest risk

Agreeing tax wording under time pressure that converts a pass-through tax into your cost. The control is a pre-closing tax review: your lawyer and indirect tax adviser read the final draft's tax clause against the tax map before the meeting, and you bring a written list of the points you will not concede. Professional sign-off required: a real estate lawyer and an indirect tax specialist.

The beginner's mistake

Treating the allocation as the buyer's business. It is half of a trade, and it has a price.

Callback

In week 3 you studied anchoring: the first number on the table pulls everything toward it. "Inclusive of all taxes" is an anchor dressed as housekeeping. And in week 6, the habit of saying "I'll confirm by Friday" applies here in miniature: "Let me check that against our numbers" buys the minute you need without a confrontation.

Recap

Price exclusive of indirect tax. Tax collected at closing, not indemnified. An allocation that costs you nothing is still worth trading. Find the cash-flow problem behind the request and solve it rather than inherit it. Walk-away points on one card, and a calm voice.

Next: Kema, Quiz and Recap, on the real estate tax map.
checklist: Have the tax clause reviewed against the tax map before the closing meeting
Write your walk-away points on one card
Insist the price is stated exclusive of indirect tax, with each portion's treatment
Collect indirect and transfer tax through the trust account at closing
Know what each allocation costs you before you are asked
Trade any concession of value for something in return
Add a cooperation clause for consistent filing
head: Field checklist
speak: At the closing table, the buyer's lawyer may ask for three things that sound like housekeeping. First, a price inclusive of all taxes. On a taxable portion, that means the tax comes out of your price, so say the agreed price is the price of the property, with indirect tax in addition. Second, a larger allocation to the building. If your numbers show it costs you nothing, accept it, but say it is valuable to their client and ask what you get in return, then stay silent. Third, an indemnity instead of collecting tax at closing. An indemnity moves the cost but not the liability, so insist it is paid through the trust account. Behind each request is a real need, usually cash at closing. Solve that need rather than inherit the risk. Bring your walk-away points on a card, and take a short break whenever you need to check a number.
terms: Walk-away point — a term you have decided in advance not to concede
Cooperation clause — a contract term requiring both parties to file consistently and share information on tax treatment
Holdback — part of the price retained at closing as security for later obligations

hostile.q: Every seller in this market accepts tax-inclusive pricing. Why are you holding up the closing over it?
hostile.a: I'm not holding it up; I'm making sure we close on the price we agreed. Fourteen million was the price of the property. If tax applies to part of it, it is in addition, collected at closing and remitted correctly. That protects your client too, because consistent treatment is what both of our filings will rely on.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: The real estate tax map: the week in six questions
summary: Six questions on transfer tax, indirect tax recoverability, recapture and allocation; a Red Pen drill on a pro forma with planted tax defects; and a two-minute boardroom explanation of the tax map.
body:
Mr Shabazz, this week's whole idea fits on one sheet of paper: four moments, three taxes, every cell filled in before you price. Today we test that you can draw it, catch the errors in someone else's version, and explain it in two minutes.

Recall

Q. Why does unrecoverable indirect tax cut yield on cost?

A. Because it adds to total project cost without adding to net operating income. In the hypothetical 60-unit example, it took yield on cost from about 6.89 percent to about 6.40 percent.

Q. What is the difference between joint and several liability and proportionate liability?

A. Under joint and several liability, each liable party can be made to pay the whole loss and must chase the others; under proportionate liability, each pays only its share. Which applies varies by jurisdiction and claim.

Q. What is the IRR trap of a short hold?

A. A quick deal can show a very high IRR on a small profit, so a project can win on IRR while making far less money than a slower one with a lower IRR.

Why this matters

Transaction taxes are where competent developers lose money they never knew they had. The ideas are simple; the discipline of applying them before signing is what is rare. If you can do today's drills fluently, you will catch these errors in your team's work and in counterparties' drafts.

The six questions

Question 1. What are the four moments and three taxes on the real estate tax map? Answer: acquisition, construction, operation and exit; transfer tax, indirect tax and income tax. Each cell records who pays, on what amount, when, and whether it is recoverable.

Question 2. Why can the same construction cost carry different tax depending on the building's use? Answer: because input tax is usually recoverable when you make taxable supplies, such as many commercial rents, and usually not recoverable when you make exempt supplies, such as many long-term residential rents. The rules differ by country and must be verified.

Question 3. What is recapture? Answer: taxing back, as income, depreciation previously deducted, to the extent the sale shows the building did not lose that value. It is often capped at the building's original cost.

Question 4. What does Rule 23 say, and what failure produced it? Answer: no price quoted and no transfer signed until the tax map for that transaction is written down. It came from a composite case where two land transfers, tax-inclusive pre-sale prices and partly unrecoverable input tax consumed most of a project's margin.

Question 5. Can a contract make the buyer liable to the authority for a tax the statute places on the seller? Answer: generally no. The statute fixes legal liability; the contract can move the economic burden. If the other party fails to pay, the authority usually still pursues the person the statute names, so collect tax at closing.

Question 6. Why do buyer and seller disagree about the purchase price allocation? Answer: depreciation is claimed on buildings, not land. The seller often prefers less on the building to limit recapture; the buyer prefers more for future depreciation. Support the allocation with a valuation and file consistently.

Say that out loud now.

Red Pen drill

Here is a hypothetical pro forma excerpt with notes. Find the defects before reading on.

"Land 3,000,000 (transfer tax nil, as the land moves from our holding company to the project company). Hard costs 12,000,000 net of value-added tax, which we will recover. Use: 80 long-term rental apartments. Contingency 5 percent, also covering any tax surprises. Sales of the 10 townhouses at the rear priced at 600,000 each, all-in. Exit: building sold in year 7, tax at 20 percent of the gain. Allocation of exit price to be agreed with the buyer after closing."

The defects. One: transfer tax assumed nil on a move between related companies, with no confirmation that a relief applies and its conditions are met. Two: value-added tax assumed recoverable on a building whose main use is long-term residential rental, which is often exempt; the unrecoverable tax should be a cost line. Three: contingency used to absorb computable taxes; a tax you can compute is not an unknown. Four: townhouses priced all-in, so revenue must be the price less the indirect tax inside it, if new homes are taxable there. Five: exit tax as a single rate on the gain, ignoring recapture of depreciation. Six: allocation left until after closing, when it can no longer be negotiated. Seven, a quiet one: no line for the timing gap on any recoverable tax.

Boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes to an investment committee. Time it, then compare.

"Before we price this deal, we have mapped every tax at four moments. At acquisition, transfer tax is in the land cost, and we have confirmed whether the move into the project company attracts it. During construction, the residential portion's indirect tax is shown as a cost, because those rents are expected to be exempt; the commercial portion is shown as recoverable, with the timing gap financed. While operating, property tax is an expense, and income tax runs below the line. At exit, we model recapture separately from the capital gain, and we have tested how the land and building allocation changes our tax and the buyer's, so we know what it is worth in negotiation. Prices are stated exclusive of indirect tax, and tax is collected at closing. All rates are provisional and are being verified by an indirect tax specialist and a tax adviser."

Scoring your answer

Score 1 to 5 on accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question. The hard question this week is the one investors rarely ask but always need: "what tax do we pay before there is any profit?" If your answer covered it without prompting, give yourself the point.

Draw it from memory

One more drill, the most useful of the week. Take a blank sheet. Without looking, draw the four-by-three map and fill each cell for a hypothetical building you invent: a small office building, or 20 apartments, or a row of townhouses for sale. Then check each cell against this week's lessons. Where you hesitated, write the question you would ask an adviser. Most people find two or three cells they cannot fill. Those cells are your homework, and they are exactly the questions to put on your next adviser's engagement letter, which is next fortnight's subject.

When you check your map, use this order: first the transfer taxes, because they are paid first and are the easiest to miss on internal moves; then the indirect tax cells, split by use; then income tax at exit, including recapture. Order matters because the earliest taxes are the ones with the least time to fix.

Then do the same exercise with a partner or a friend: hand them your map and ask them to find one cell you got wrong. Explaining why a cell says what it says is the fastest way to discover whether you understand it or have only memorised it.

The biggest risk

Knowing the map and still not drawing it on a busy week. The control is a habit: the tax map is a required attachment to every go or no-go memo, every land agreement and every sales price list, and no document goes out without it.

The beginner's mistake

Assuming the lawyer will catch the tax clause. Lawyers catch what they are asked to review; ask explicitly.

Callback

Week 15 introduced leakage, and last week explained income tax character. This week added the taxes that arrive before profit and at exit. Together they mean the after-tax return is built from at least five lines, not one, and every one of them is set by a choice you make early.

Recap

Four moments, three taxes. Use decides recoverability. Recapture comes back at exit. The statute fixes liability; the contract moves burden. Allocation is a trade with a price. Rule 23 puts the map before the price.

head: The six questions
speak: This week fits on one page: four moments, three taxes. At acquisition, transfer tax hits at closing, including on moves between your own companies unless a relief applies. During construction, value-added tax is recoverable if you make taxable supplies, and a real cost if your rents are exempt, which is common for long-term residential. While you operate, property tax is an expense and income tax runs below the line. At exit, the gain may be capital, but depreciation you claimed can come back as recapture, taxed as income. The statute decides who is liable; the contract only moves who bears it, so collect tax at closing. The split of the price between land and building pits seller against buyer, so support it with a valuation and trade it for something. And Rule 23: no price quoted and no transfer signed until the tax map is written down.
terms: Exempt supply — a supply on which no indirect tax is charged and on which input tax is usually not recoverable
Zero-rated supply — a supply taxed at zero, on which input tax is usually recoverable
Change of use — converting property to a use with different tax treatment, which can claw back past input tax credits

hostile.q: Your model assumes the move into the project company is free of transfer tax. On what basis?
hostile.a: On written advice that a relief for related-company transfers applies, with its conditions listed in the appendix and confirmed against the corporate chart. If any condition fails, the tax is about 90,000 on this land at the hypothetical working rate, and that figure is shown as a downside in the sensitivity table.
